text:
Members of the jury, this is not a case where the Prosecution can prove beyond reasonable doubt that these two officers’ conduct, and not the ANL’s own late and ambiguous manoeuvres, criminally caused the deaths under s 304A of the Penal Code. On 3 January 2003, RSS *Courageous* was carrying out a naval patrol near Pedra Branca, and a Navy minute dated 27 January 2003 confirms that RSN patrol craft may, for operational reasons, legitimately position themselves against the general traffic flow in that area; the mere fact of the turnaround was therefore not itself unlawful or reckless. You will hear that the bridge team had been trained to regard a 3-cable CPA as operationally acceptable if monitored, that the first appellant was entitled to supervise rather than immediately override the trainee OOW, and that the ANL’s two starboard alterations were entered incrementally on autopilot at a limited rate of turn, making them difficult to detect and depriving *Courageous* of a clear warning in the short closing time. Our case is simple: there were errors, but criminal negligence causing death requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of a grossly blameworthy act causing the fatal collision, and the evidence will show a fast-developing encounter, shared navigational fault, and at the very least a reasonable doubt that these appellants are criminally liable.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified)]

Members of the jury, this was not an unavoidable “fast-developing” tragedy: it was a collision brought about by repeated negligent decisions on board *RSS Courageous* after clear warning signs. The technical logs show that from about 11.29pm the *ANL Indonesia* remained on *Courageous*’ port bow, and that a starboard alteration of about 20° at 11.30pm would have opened the CPA to more than 0.8 nautical miles; instead, the bridge team made successive port alterations at 11.30pm, 11.31pm, 11.33pm and 11.34pm, progressively driving the CPA down to zero. The evidence will also show that the radar plotter, Second Sergeant Goh Chun Yong, had in fact appreciated from his radar presentation that the ANL was on the port side, yet no independent visual bearing check was ordered, and the Commanding Officer’s own standing orders requiring early reporting, independent verification, and avoidance of crossing ahead of large merchant traffic were not followed. Under s 304A of the Penal Code, those rash or negligent acts—persisting in wrong-way navigation in a traffic lane, failing to verify contradictory indications, and repeatedly turning to port into a 293.5m container ship until collision became inevitable—caused the deaths of four servicewomen, and the Prosecution will prove that beyond reasonable doubt.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified)]

ANL bridge movement records and manufacturer material for the vessel's autopilot/heading control system showing that the two starboard alterations were entered as incremental heading changes several minutes apart and executed at a limited rate of turn; accompanying defense analysis says the resulting manoeuvre would not have been readily apparent on another vessel's radar in the short closing time available.

The Defence’s new point about the ANL’s autopilot and limited rate of turn does not create a reasonable doubt, because it answers the wrong question. The collision was set in motion before the ANL’s starboard alterations: from 11.30pm onward, Courageous herself made repeated port alterations on the mistaken premise that the ANL was at “green 10”, and those own-ship turns are what progressively collapsed the CPA. Even if the ANL’s later response was gradual or hard to detect, that cannot excuse the Courageous bridge team’s earlier negligence in turning the wrong way into danger and then persisting with further port alterations instead of stopping, verifying the bearing, or turning starboard.

The Prosecution’s strongest point is that the bridge team’s port alterations from 11.30pm onward must, by themselves, amount to criminal causation; but that skips over the real issue in a s 304A case—whether the Prosecution has excluded a reasonable doubt that the deaths were caused by these appellants’ negligence, rather than by a collision sequence materially shaped by the ANL’s own response. The evidence already on record shows the ANL did not make one clear, bold avoiding manoeuvre: between 11.32pm and 11.34pm she entered two incremental starboard heading changes on autopilot, executed at a limited rate of turn, so that in the very short closing time they would not have been readily apparent on Courageous’ radar as a decisive alteration. Once the Prosecution accepts that ANL’s avoiding action was late, gradual and ambiguous, it cannot then say beyond reasonable doubt that the fatal impact was solely the product of the appellants’ earlier error rather than a shared, fast-developing navigational failure in which the stand-on vessel’s own manoeuvre deprived Courageous of a clear cue and a real chance to recover.
[Law-library check: s 304A (verified)]

Radar and ARPA data extraction report prepared by the RSN technical branch from the Courageous' equipment logs, showing that from about 11.29pm onward the ANL's relative track remained on the Courageous' port bow and that a starboard alteration of about 20° at 11.30pm would have opened the CPA to more than 0.8nm, whereas the actual port alterations progressively reduced CPA to zero.

Defense expert Captain John Third's report, including simulator runs, concluding that the Courageous' first two port alterations should be treated as a single developing manoeuvre intended to cross ahead, and that if the ANL had immediately disengaged autopilot and applied a single substantial starboard helm of about 30° to 40° when danger became apparent, the vessels would likely have cleared each other.

Under s 304A of the Penal Code, the Prosecution must prove that the deaths were caused by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide; on these facts, that act was the Courageous bridge team’s repeated and unjustified port alterations into danger after the risk was already apparent. The defence expert’s theory that ANL could still have avoided collision with a larger 30°–40° starboard turn does not break causation: even if ANL might have done more, the appellants had already, from 11.30pm onward, turned the wrong way on a false bearing, reducing the CPA from 0.3nm to zero when the RSN logs show a 20° starboard turn would instead have opened it to over 0.8nm. In law and common sense, a victim vessel’s allegedly imperfect evasive action is not a reasonable doubt where the accused’s own negligent navigation remained an operating and substantial cause of the deaths right up to the 11.35pm impact.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified)]

Under s 304A of the Penal Code, the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that these appellants caused the deaths by a rash or negligent act; it is not enough to show an error of seamanship if causation remains reasonably doubtful. On the Prosecution’s own timeline, the collision occurred only after ANL’s officers recognised danger at about 11.32pm and then chose two incremental autopilot starboard heading changes between 11.32pm and 11.34pm, while our expert Captain John Third concluded that an immediate substantial starboard helm of about 30° to 40° would likely have cleared the vessels. So even if the Courageous bridge team was mistaken at 11.30pm, s 304A is not made out unless the Prosecution excludes the reasonable possibility that ANL’s late, gradual and ambiguous avoiding action was a concurrent operative cause of the fatal impact at 11.35pm; on this record, it has not done so.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified); s 304A (verified)]

Certified copy of the Commanding Officer's standing night orders and bridge standing orders for RSS Courageous containing instructions that in any close-quarters situation in the TSS the OOW is to call the CO early, verify contact bearings by independent means, and avoid crossing ahead of large merchant traffic unless safe passing is certain; the bridge log shows no call to the CO until the danger had become acute.

Statement from a former Courageous bridge crew member who had served with both appellants on prior patrols, saying the first appellant's usual practice was to allow the trainee OOW to con the ship unless there was a plainly unsafe order, and that the second appellant had previously handled turnarounds at the patrol limit without incident; the defense relies on this to support that the first appellant had reason to trust her handling and that the second appellant was acting within the scope of her supervised training rather than independently disregarding procedure.

Under s 304A of the Penal Code, the Prosecution need only prove that the deaths were caused by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide; it is no answer that another vessel might also have acted imperfectly if the appellants’ negligence remained an operating and substantial cause. Here, the proved negligence is concrete and repeated: despite the CPA alarm at 0.3nm, the standing orders required the OOW to call the CO early, verify bearings independently, and avoid crossing ahead unless safe passing was certain, yet no such verification or timely call was made and Courageous altered to port at 11.30pm, 11.31pm, 11.33pm and 11.34pm on a false premise while the RSN radar/ARPA logs show the ANL remained on the port bow and that a 20° starboard turn at 11.30pm would have opened CPA to over 0.8nm. So even taking the Defence case at its highest—that ANL could have made a larger starboard turn—the appellants’ own negligent navigation was still a direct, continuing cause of the 11.35pm collision and the four deaths, satisfying s 304A beyond reasonable doubt.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified); s 304A (verified)]

Under s 304A of the Penal Code, the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the deaths were caused by a rash or negligent act of these appellants; where the evidence is equally consistent with a tragic navigational error made in the course of duty, or with concurrent causation by the other vessel’s response, that criminal standard is not met. Here, the Prosecution’s own case accepts that the encounter developed over minutes from about 11.30pm to 11.35pm, and the Defence evidence on record shows ANL’s avoiding action was not a single bold helm order but two incremental autopilot starboard changes between 11.32pm and 11.34pm at a limited rate of turn, while Captain Third’s evidence is that an immediate substantial 30°–40° starboard helm would likely have avoided impact; that leaves a real doubt whether the fatalities were proved to have been caused, in the criminal sense required by s 304A of the Penal Code, by these officers’ conduct alone rather than by a shared and fast-developing collision sequence. The standing orders and ARPA reconstruction may show negligence in hindsight, but s 304A punishes proved criminal causation, not every operational misjudgment at sea, and on this record the Prosecution has not excluded the reasonable possibility that ANL’s late and ambiguous manoeuvre was an operative cause of the collision.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified); s 304A (verified)]

MPA inquiry interview transcript of Second Sergeant Goh Chun Yong recorded on 9 January 2003 stating that when the CPA alarm activated he reported the ANL as bearing on the Courageous' port side based on his radar presentation, but after the petty OOW immediately echoed 'green 10' he did not challenge the bridge team further because events were unfolding quickly; the transcript also notes that no one on the bridge ordered a visual bearing check after the contradictory indications.

Extracts from RSS Courageous training records and the CO's night order book for the six weeks before the collision showing repeated acceptance of CPAs in the 0.2 to 0.3nm range during patrol operations with merchant traffic, with no recorded criticism from supervising officers; the defense uses this to show the bridge team had been trained that a 3-cable CPA was operationally acceptable if monitored.

The Defence’s latest reliance on prior training records accepting 0.2–0.3nm CPAs does not answer the actual negligence proved here, because this was not a stable, monitored passing in ordinary patrol conditions. At 11.29pm–11.30pm the CPA alarm had already activated, the bridge had contradictory indications about whether ANL was on the port or starboard side, no independent visual bearing check was ordered, no early call was made to the CO despite standing orders, and yet Courageous still altered to port repeatedly at 11.30pm, 11.31pm, 11.33pm and 11.34pm; the RSN ARPA logs show those port turns reduced CPA to zero, while a 20° starboard turn at 11.30pm would have opened it to over 0.8nm. So the issue is not whether 3 cables could ever be acceptable in some training context, but that these appellants treated a close-quarters alarm as acceptable while acting on an unverified false bearing and manoeuvring the wrong way into a 293.5m container ship.

Members of the jury, under **s 304A of the Penal Code**, the Prosecution must prove **beyond reasonable doubt** that these appellants’ conduct was the criminal cause of the four deaths, not merely that mistakes were made in a difficult bridge situation. The evidence leaves that doubt: the **Office of the Chief of Navy minute dated 27 January 2003, “Compliance with COLREGS,”** expressly states that RSN patrol craft near **Pedra Branca** may, because of operational requirements, **legitimately position themselves against the general flow** where mission needs and local safety assessments require it, so the 11.25pm turnaround itself was not unlawful rashness; and the training records show a **0.2–0.3nm CPA** had repeatedly been treated as operationally acceptable if monitored.  

The Prosecution’s best point is the sequence of port alterations at **11.30pm, 11.31pm, 11.33pm and 11.34pm**, but even there criminal causation is not proved: the bridge was acting in a fast-closing encounter at about **31 knots**, the ANL’s own records show her response was **two incremental autopilot starboard changes between 11.32pm and 11.34pm** at a limited rate of turn, and Captain Third’s evidence is that an immediate **30°–40° starboard helm** would likely have avoided collision. Once you accept that ANL’s avoiding action was late, gradual and not readily apparent, and that these officers were operating within training and naval patrol practice rather than in conscious disregard of safety, the case becomes one of tragic shared navigational failure—not proof beyond reasonable doubt of a **rash or negligent act causing death** under s 304A. Your verdict must therefore be for the accused.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified); s 304A (verified)]

Members of the jury, **s 304A of the Penal Code** is satisfied where death is caused by a rash or negligent act, and the Prosecution has proved that beyond reasonable doubt: after the CPA alarm at **0.3nm**, with closing speed about **31 knots**, the Courageous bridge ignored standing orders to **call the CO early, verify bearings independently, and avoid crossing ahead unless safe**, even though Second Sergeant Goh’s **9 January 2003** MPA interview confirms he had in fact appreciated from radar that **ANL was on the port side** and no visual bearing check was ever ordered. The technical evidence is one-way: the RSN radar/ARPA logs show that from about **11.29pm** ANL stayed on the **port bow**, that a **20° starboard** alteration at **11.30pm** would have opened CPA to **more than 0.8nm**, yet the Courageous instead turned **to port four times**—**235° to 215° at 11.30pm, to 210° at 11.31pm, to 200° at 11.33pm, and to 190° at 11.34pm**—driving CPA to zero. Captain Hilbert Fernandez’s reconstruction explains why the Defence’s “3 cables was acceptable” point fails: in a night, near-head-on encounter with a **293.5m** container ship, **0.3nm was below prudent margin** because of radar lag, target aspect changes and the ANL’s turning characteristics, so this was never a safe monitored pass. And the Defence’s best causation point—that ANL could have made a bigger starboard turn—does not raise a reasonable doubt, because Master Koop’s statement, bell book and autopilot printout show ANL gave an **attention whistle** and altered starboard in two steps only after Courageous stopped presenting a stable port-to-port aspect, while **no whistle or manoeuvring signal came from Courageous before impact**; ANL’s imperfect last-minute response did not break causation where the appellants’ own negligent navigation remained the direct, operating cause of the collision and the four deaths.
[Law-library check: s 304A of the Penal Code (verified)]

variables.cause: Criminal -- s 304A of the Penal Code (Causing death by rash or negligent act)
variables.facts:
2 Both the appellants are lieutenants in the Republic of Singapore Navy (“RSN”). The charges against them arose out of the tragic collision between the RSN ship RSS Courageous (“the Courageous”) and the merchant vessel ANL Indonesia (“the ANL”) on 3 January 2003, which resulted in the deaths of four RSN servicewomen.

The vessels
3 The ANL was a Netherlands-registered container ship with a gross tonnage of 51,938. She was 293.5m in length and had a top speed of 24.8 knots (46km/h). The Courageous was a “Fearless Class” anti-submarine patrol vessel which displaced approximately 452 tonnes. At 57.94m, she was less than one-fifth the length of the ANL. She was powered by an advanced twin jet propulsion system, and had a top speed exceeding 20 knots (37km/h).
4 Both ships were equipped with a Gyro compass, radar, Automatic Radar Plotting Aid and other navigational equipment and charts. All the equipment was functioning at the material time.

The sequence of events
5 At about 11.20pm on 3 January 2003, the Courageous and the ANL were both travelling on the eastbound lane of the Traffic Separation Scheme (“TSS”) just off the Horsburgh Lighthouse at Pedra Branca. Both vessels were moving in a north-easterly direction in accordance with the general traffic flow. The ANL was en route from Port Klang, Malaysia, to Busan, South Korea, while the Courageous was some 6 nautical miles (“nm”) ahead of the ANL conducting her regular patrol of the waters.
6 At the material time, the first appellant was the Officer-of-the-Watch (“OOW”) on the Courageous. He was responsible for the safe navigation of the ship. The second appellant was only a trainee OOW, but she had the con, or control of the steering, of the vessel. She made navigational decisions and issued the relevant orders to the rest of the bridge team. As the supervising OOW, the first appellant would only intervene if he was of the view that any of her actions or instructions were wrong.
7 At 11.25pm, the Courageous reached the end of her patrol area. After checking that both sides were clear, the second appellant ordered the Courageous to execute a “U-turn”. This changed her course to a south-westerly direction of 235°, leading her to proceed down the eastbound lane of the TSS against the general flow of traffic.
8 Shortly after, the officer on the bridge of the ANL, Gerrit Easge Botma (“Botma”), observed the red port sidelight of the Courageous on the port side of the ANL. This suggested that the vessels would pass port to port. Meanwhile, on board the Courageous, the Closest Point of Approach (“CPA”) alarm on the radar came on. The CPA alarm was set at three cables (0.3nm), indicating that the closest distance at which the Courageous would pass the target vessel (the ANL) was about three cables.
9 Second Sergeant Goh Chun Yong, the radar plotter on the Courageous, reported the activation of the CPA alarm to the second appellant and informed her that the ANL was at “green 10” (10° on the starboard side). The lookout, First Sergeant Tan Soon Teck, and the petty OOW, Marcus Kuah Yeow Hwee, both confirmed his report. At this time, the vessels were closing in on each other at 31 knots or five cables per minute. Based on the report from the bridge team that the ANL was on the starboard side of the Courageous, the second appellant ordered an alteration to port from 235° to 215° at 11.30pm to increase the CPA. She also ordered a reduction in speed from Step 4 (1,000rpm or 13 knots) to Step 3 (860rpm or 12 knots).
10 Unfortunately, neither the appellants nor the rest of the bridge team realised that the ANL was in fact on the port side of the Courageous. The latter’s alteration to port therefore inadvertently brought the courses of the vessels even closer together. When the CPA did not open up as the second appellant had hoped, she ordered a further alteration to port from 215° to 210° at 11.31pm.
11 A minute later, Botma saw the green starboard light of the Courageous and realised that she had altered to port. As her relative bearing was not changing and the CPA was now zero, Botma alerted the Captain of the ANL, Petrus Paulaus Maria Koop (“Koop”), to the danger of collision. After a quick discussion, they decided to alter the ANL’s course to starboard in accordance with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972 (“the Collision Regulations”). The ANL made two alterations to starboard by autopilot between 11.32pm and 11.34pm, bringing her course from 51° to 73°. She also sounded a whistle blast to alert the Courageous.
12 At 11.33pm, the second appellant ordered the Courageous to make yet another alteration to port to 200°. She also ordered the speed to be increased back to Step 4. At 11.34pm, she ordered a final alteration to port to 190°, followed shortly by an order to put the helm hard to port. The first appellant also ordered both engines to “full throttle”.
13 The combination of the ANL’s alterations to starboard and the Courageous’ alterations to port resulted in the vessels colliding at 11.35pm about 1nm northeast of the Horsburgh Lighthouse. The ANL sustained superficial damage to her bow area, and none of her crew of 23 were injured. However, the Courageous sustained heavy losses. Part of her aft section was sheared off and sank. Of her 44 crewmembers, eight were injured and four died.
variables.plaintiff_claim: The Prosecution charges the accused with an offence under s 304A of the Penal Code (Causing death by rash or negligent act) on the facts of this case.
variables.standard: Standard of proof: the Prosecution must prove every element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt; the accused need only raise a reasonable doubt and need not prove innocence. A statutory presumption (for example the presumption of trafficking under s 17 of the Misuse of Drugs Act) shifts a burden to the accused only once the Prosecution has proved the facts that trigger it, and the accused then rebuts it on a balance of probabilities. Where a reasonable doubt remains, find for the accused.
